title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
directAnswer: A Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) answers prefix-sum queries and point updates in O(log n) each, using a single array and one bit trick. Each index i is responsible for a block of `lowbit(i) = i & -i` elements ending at i. To query prefix(i), jump i down by removing its lowest set bit each step; to update index i, jump up by adding its lowest set bit. It is shorter than a segment tree for the point-update + prefix-sum case. Use 1-based indexing.

remember.pattern: Implicit tree over an array via the lowest-set-bit (i & -i) jump
remember.formula:
update(i, delta):           # i is 1-based
    while i <= n: bit[i] += delta; i += i & -i
prefix(i):                  # sum of a[1..i]
    s = 0
    while i > 0: s += bit[i]; i -= i & -i
    return s
rules: Use **1-based** indexing — index 0 has `lowbit(0) = 0`, which would loop forever.
`lowbit(i) = i & -i` isolates the **lowest set bit**; that value is the size of the block node i covers.
**update** climbs by `i += i & -i` (toward n); **query** descends by `i -= i & -i` (toward 0). Opposite directions.
A range sum `[l, r]` is `prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1)` — two prefix queries.
Store **deltas** in update: `bit[i] += delta`, not `= val`. To set a value, first compute the difference from the current value.
whenToUse: Point updates plus prefix-sum (or range-sum) queries, interleaved
Counting inversions, or 'how many seen so far are ≤ x' while streaming
Coordinate-compressed frequency counts with running totals
When you want segment-tree power for sums but with shorter, cache-friendly code
antiSignals: Need range min/max, not sum → Fenwick does not support arbitrary range min cleanly; use a segment tree
Need range updates + range queries → a lazy segment tree is the cleaner fit (or a two-BIT trick)
Array is static → a prefix-sum array gives O(1) queries with no structure
Non-invertible aggregate (e.g. max with deletions) → prefix subtraction breaks down
remember.takeaway: The Fenwick tree is the minimalist's segment tree for sums: one array, two five-line loops, and the `i & -i` trick that lets each index own a power-of-two-sized block. It trades the segment tree's generality for half the code and a smaller constant factor.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand the lowbit decomposition — that index i covers the block of size i & -i ending at i — and can explain why update and query walk in opposite directions, all on 1-based indices.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using 0-based indexing so lowbit(0) = 0 spins forever, or moving in the wrong direction (descending on update), or storing absolute values instead of deltas.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the structure from the binary representation: prefix(i) splits into O(log n) blocks, one per set bit of i. Mention that two Fenwick trees give range-update + range-query, and that it is the standard tool for counting inversions.

problemStatement:
Maintain a Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) over an array `a[1..n]` supporting:

1. ***update(i, delta)*** — add `delta` to `a[i]`.
2. ***prefix(i)*** — return `a[1] + a[2] + … + a[i]`.
3. ***rangeSum(l, r)*** — return `a[l] + … + a[r]`, computed as `prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1)`.

Each of the first two operations must run in ***O(log n)***. Explain the `lowbit = i & -i` trick that makes this work.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ (or larger; the structure scales to ~10⁶ comfortably)
Indices are 1-based: valid i is in [1, n]
Up to 10⁵ interleaved update and query calls
Sums fit in 64-bit (use long in Java)
understanding: We want prefix sums that survive point updates without an O(n) rebuild. A Fenwick tree assigns to each index i responsibility for a contiguous block of `i & -i` elements ending at i. Because every prefix `[1, i]` decomposes into exactly the blocks indicated by the set bits of i, a prefix query reads O(log n) cells, and a point update touches the O(log n) blocks that contain that index.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array indexed from 0 or 1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 1-based for the Fenwick tree itself. Index 0 has lowbit 0, which makes the update loop never advance — so I shift external 0-based indices by +1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are updates 'add delta' or 'set value'?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The primitive is 'add delta'. To set a[i] = v, compute delta = v − current(i) and add that. Storing absolute values directly would corrupt the partial sums.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need range min/max too?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — Fenwick excels at invertible aggregates like sum and xor. For range min/max use a segment tree, since prefix subtraction does not recover a min.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The loops are O(log n) and the array is size n+1, so n up to ~10⁶ is comfortable. No recursion, so no stack-depth concern.

approaches.name: Baseline — Prefix-Sum Array (Rebuild on Update)
approaches.whenToMention: State this first: it is the obvious structure and it exposes exactly which operation hurts, motivating the BIT.
hints: Precompute prefix[i] = a[1] + … + a[i]. Then prefix(i) is a single array read — O(1).
But update(i, delta) changes a[i], which shifts prefix[i], prefix[i+1], …, prefix[n] — every later prefix. That is O(n) per update.
Symmetrically, storing the raw array makes updates O(1) but queries O(n). Neither is good when both operations are frequent.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A prefix-sum array answers queries by one read (O(1)) but any single update invalidates all suffix prefixes, costing O(n) to repair. With q updates that is O(q·n).
approaches.explanation:
The first idea for prefix sums is a precomputed prefix array.

**Queries are instant.** With `prefix[i]` stored, `prefix(i)` is one array read — O(1). For a static array this is unbeatable.

**Updates are the problem.** Changing `a[i]` by `delta` changes every prefix from `i` onward: `prefix[i], prefix[i+1], …, prefix[n]` all increase by `delta`. Repairing them is an O(n) sweep.

**Why this fails the problem.** The operations are interleaved and there are up to 10⁵ updates. Each O(n) repair gives up to 10¹⁰ total work. The plain (non-prefix) array flips the costs — O(1) update, O(n) query — but is equally bad when queries are frequent.

**What the Fenwick tree fixes.** We want *both* sub-linear. The BIT stores partial sums over power-of-two-sized blocks so that an update touches only the O(log n) blocks containing index i, and a query reads only the O(log n) blocks that tile `[1, i]`.
approaches.insight: The prefix-sum array and the raw array are the two extremes: O(1)/O(n) and O(n)/O(1). The Fenwick tree pays a logarithm on both sides by chopping the prefix into blocks whose sizes are powers of two — exactly the set bits of the index.

approaches.name: Fenwick Tree — lowbit Jumps (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for point update + prefix sum. 'Each index owns a block of i & -i elements; update climbs, query descends.'

complexity.time: O(n) build, O(log n) update, O(log n) query

hints: Give index i responsibility for the block of elements ending at i with length lowbit(i) = i & -i (the value of its lowest set bit).
To query prefix(i), repeatedly add bit[i] and strip the lowest set bit: i -= i & -i, until i hits 0. The blocks visited tile [1, i] exactly.
To update index i, repeatedly add delta to bit[i] and add the lowest set bit: i += i & -i, until i exceeds n. Those are the blocks that contain i.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Stripping or adding the lowest set bit changes the number of set bits / magnitude so that at most O(log n) iterations occur (one per bit position). Each iteration is O(1). Build can be done in O(n) by propagating each value to its parent, or O(n log n) by n updates.
approaches.explanation:
A Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) is an array `bit[1..n]` where each index secretly owns a block of consecutive elements, and the block boundaries come straight from binary representation.

**The lowbit idea.** Define `lowbit(i) = i & -i`. In two's complement, `-i` flips all bits of `i` and adds 1, so `i & -i` isolates the *lowest set bit* of `i`. For example `lowbit(6) = lowbit(110₂) = 010₂ = 2`. We declare that `bit[i]` stores the sum of the block `a[i − lowbit(i) + 1 .. i]` — a run of `lowbit(i)` elements ending at `i`. So `bit[4]` (lowbit 4) covers `[1,4]`, `bit[6]` (lowbit 2) covers `[5,6]`, `bit[7]` (lowbit 1) covers `[7,7]`.

**Why a prefix query is O(log n).** To get `prefix(i) = a[1..i]`, start at `i` and add `bit[i]` (the block ending at `i`), then jump to `i − lowbit(i)` — the index just before that block — and repeat. Each jump removes the lowest set bit, so the number of jumps equals the number of set bits in `i`, at most `log₂ n`. The blocks visited are disjoint and tile `[1, i]` perfectly. For `i = 7 = 111₂` we read `bit[7]` (size 1), `bit[6]` (size 2), `bit[4]` (size 4) — three reads for a 7-element prefix.

**Why a point update is O(log n).** Adding `delta` to `a[i]` must update every block that *contains* `i`. Those are found by repeatedly adding the lowest set bit: `i, i + lowbit(i), …`. Each step moves to the next-larger block that swallows the current one, and again there are at most `log₂ n` such blocks before exceeding `n`. Update climbs; query descends — opposite directions over the same lowbit step.

**Why 1-based indexing is mandatory.** `lowbit(0) = 0`, so an update starting at index 0 would do `i += 0` forever. Anchoring the tree at index 1 (and shifting any external 0-based index by +1) avoids the infinite loop and makes the block math clean.

**Range sums by subtraction.** Because sum is invertible, `rangeSum(l, r) = prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1)`. This is exactly why Fenwick trees are restricted to invertible aggregates: you cannot recover a range *minimum* by subtracting two prefix minima.
approaches.insight: The whole structure is binary arithmetic in disguise: the set bits of an index tell you both how to split a prefix into blocks (query, descending) and which blocks own an element (update, ascending). That single `i & -i` operation replaces all the explicit child/parent pointers a segment tree needs — which is why the code is so short and the constant factor so small.

edgeCases.behavior: Bug trap: lowbit(0) = 0 means i never advances → infinite loop. Always keep the tree 1-based.
Loop condition i > 0 is immediately false → returns 0, the correct empty-prefix sum.
prefix(n) − prefix(0) = whole-array sum; prefix(0) safely returns 0.

pitfalls: 0-based indexing — lowbit(0) = 0 causes the update loop to never terminate.
Swapping the directions — climbing on query or descending on update gives wrong sums.
Storing absolute values in update instead of deltas — compute delta = new − old to set a value.
Using int for sums in Java when totals exceed 2³¹ — use long.

commonMistakes: Using 0-based indices, so lowbit(0) = 0 makes the update loop spin forever.
Moving in the wrong direction: query must descend (strip lowbit), update must climb (add lowbit).
Passing an absolute value to update instead of a delta.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Zero-based indexing infinite loop
commonMistakesDetailed.why: lowbit(0) = 0 & -0 = 0, so 'i += i & -i' leaves i at 0 forever. The Fenwick tree must be 1-based; shift any external 0-based index by +1 before calling.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def update(self, i, delta):   # i passed as 0-based
    while i < self.n:
        self.bit[i] += delta
        i += i & -i           # i stays 0 forever when i == 0
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
def update(self, i, delta):   # i is 1-based
    while i <= self.n:
        self.bit[i] += delta
        i += i & -i

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong jump direction
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Update touches the blocks that contain i (climb by adding lowbit); query reads the blocks that tile [1, i] (descend by stripping lowbit). Swapping them reads the wrong cells and returns garbage.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Absolute value instead of delta
commonMistakesDetailed.why: update adds delta into every covering block. Passing the new absolute value double-counts the old contribution. To set a[i] = v, add v − current(i).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def set_value(self, i, v):
    self.update(i, v)            # adds v on top of the old value

patternNote: Fenwick tree / Binary Indexed Tree: an implicit tree over an array where index i owns a block of i & -i elements. Update climbs by adding the lowest set bit, prefix query descends by stripping it — both O(log n). The minimalist tool for point update + prefix/range sum on invertible aggregates (sum, xor).
